title: Puppy Potty Training Regression: Why Accidents Start Again and What to Do
description: Puppy was doing great, now accidents are back? Why potty training setbacks happen, when to call the vet, and a step-by-step reset, based on Dogs Trust and AKC.
excerpt: Why accidents can return after weeks of progress, when to call the vet, and how to reset your puppy's potty routine.
seoTitle: Puppy Potty Training Regression: Why Accidents Return
imageAlt: PuppyGuido cover: Potty Training Regression (golden retriever puppy)
html:
Setbacks are common. Dogs Trust says they are normal, especially during adolescence, and with routine changes or new environments. Preventive Vet says the whole potty training process tends to last about four to six months as your puppy matures into adolescence. First rule out a medical cause, then check what has changed, then go back to basics.

Is this normal?

Yes, often. Dogs Trust says that most dogs will be toilet trained after four to six months of consistent training, and that setbacks are normal. Preventive Vet says many puppies go through regression, and that it takes time for a puppy's body to mature. No source we read says exactly how long a setback lasts, so we won't give a number.

Step 1: Rule out a medical cause

If the accidents started suddenly, or your puppy's toilet habits have changed for no clear reason, call your vet. Dogs Trust lists these signs that may point to illness:

  • Blood in urine or stool
  • Peeing or pooping more often, or in larger amounts
  • Excessive thirst or a change in appetite
  • Straining with nothing coming out
  • Color changes in pee or poo, or worms in the poo
  • Sudden setbacks with no clear reason

Dogs Trust says common conditions include urinary tract infections, bladder stones and kidney disease. AKC says a UTI can easily lead to accidents in the house. Preventive Vet adds that for pooping accidents, causes can include intestinal parasites, or food that is too rich or too much food.

AKC says that if housetraining problems persist despite consistent training, a veterinary evaluation is the next step.

Step 2: Check what has changed

Most sources point to a few common causes:

Possible causeSource
Too much freedom too soon. Many owners expand access to the house too quickly.AKC
Old smells. Dogs often return to spots that still smell like earlier accidents. Use an enzymatic cleaner.AKC, Dogs Trust
Routine or environment changes, anxiety, or being left aloneDogs Trust
Missed signals or breaks that are too far apartAKC
Switching from pads to outside only. The puppy is learning a new habit.Preventive Vet
Scent marking, which can show up in adolescenceDogs Trust

On neutering: Dogs Trust says you can discuss it with your vet, because it may reduce inappropriate scent marking, particularly in male dogs, though some dogs still mark. We found no other source on this, so ask your vet.

Step 3: Reset the routine

This is what the sources recommend. Preventive Vet says to go back a few steps.

  1. Take your puppy out often. Dogs Trust says puppies need to go out every couple of hours, and after sleeping, playing and eating. Preventive Vet says to keep a frequent schedule until your puppy is at least six to eight months old.
  2. Supervise. Dogs Trust suggests keeping the lead on in the garden, so you can reward the moment your puppy goes.
  3. Reward right away, outside.
  4. Limit access. Use baby gates or closed doors, and a crate or puppy zone when you cannot watch (Preventive Vet, Dogs Trust). AKC suggests adding freedom one or two rooms at a time.
  5. Interrupt and take outside if you catch an accident in progress (Dogs Trust). Then clean calmly.
  6. Clean thoroughly with an enzymatic cleaner.
  7. Keep a log of accidents to find patterns (Preventive Vet).

(General guidance) Many owners find a short "reset week" helps: same potty spot, same cue, same times each day. Our potty training schedule has a sample day.

For how long a puppy can wait, see the potty training timeline and our guide to leaving a puppy alone. If your puppy refuses to go outside, see puppy won't pee outside.

What not to do

  • Do not punish. AKC says punishing accidents is less effective than rewarding correct behavior and preventing mistakes. Dogs Trust says making a big fuss or telling your dog off can make the problem worse.
  • Do not rub your puppy's nose in an accident (Preventive Vet).
  • Avoid ammonia-based cleaners (general guidance). AKC and Dogs Trust recommend enzymatic cleaners.
  • Do not limit water on your own. Dogs Trust notes that access to water must not be limited. Ask your vet if you are unsure.

When to see a professional

  • Accidents began very suddenly, or you see any signs in the Step 1 list
  • Persistent problems despite a consistent routine (AKC)
  • Your vet has ruled out medical causes. AKC suggests an experienced trainer or behaviorist next.

Dogs Trust also has a behaviour support line. This article is general information, not veterinary advice.

quick: Setbacks are normal, especially during adolescence (Dogs Trust). First rule out a medical cause with your vet, then check what changed, like too much freedom or lingering odors, and go back to basics: frequent outings, supervision and rewards.

faq.q: Why is my potty trained puppy having accidents again?
faq.a: Common reasons include a medical issue, too much freedom, routine changes, lingering odors, or scent marking in adolescence.

faq.q: Is potty training regression normal at 4 to 6 months?
faq.a: Preventive Vet says the process tends to last four to six months as puppies mature into adolescence, and that many puppies go through regression. Dogs Trust says setbacks are normal, especially during adolescence. Neither gives an exact start or end age for a setback.
We did not find a reliable figure in the sources.
It could. Dogs Trust and AKC both mention UTIs. Only a vet can diagnose it.

faq.q: Should I use pee pads again?
faq.a: We did not find a source that recommends going back to pads for regression. AKC notes pads can slow the move to outdoor toileting.
Ask your vet. Dogs Trust says it may reduce scent marking, particularly in male dogs, but some dogs still mark.
